title: Why has my pub’s business rates bill changed?
summary: A pub’s rates bill in England can change when the Valuation Office reassesses the property, when the tax multiplier changes or when the council applies different reliefs. The April 2026 revaluation raised many pub valuations. The bill depends on all three steps, so the change in rateable value alone does not tell you how much you will pay.

journey.title: From pub valuation to the bill

steps.label: Assess the premises and its trading potential
steps.text: Assess what a reasonably efficient operator could take in, by activity such as drinks, food and accommodation. Convert trading potential to an estimated annual rental value using the valuation approach for pubs.

note.heading: Why use trading potential
note.text: The Valuation Office describes a trade-based method that reflects the kind of premises and likely trade. The assessment uses the valuation date rather than the business’s takings on the day the bill arrives.

steps.label: Apply the tax rate
steps.text: The council multiplies the rateable value by the relevant multiplier to get a bill before relief. The appropriate multiplier depends on the property and financial year.

steps.label: Apply caps and discounts
steps.text: The council checks transitional support and other reliefs. For 2026–27 an eligible pub receives a further 15% discount after applicable reliefs, in the order specified by the guidance.

steps.label: Check the bill or challenge the valuation
steps.text: For a billing or relief issue contact the council. If the underlying rateable value is at issue, check the property details with the Valuation Office before challenging, with an appeal route after a challenge decision.

valuation-comparison.title: Pub rateable values rose faster than the wider sector at the 2026 revaluation
valuation-comparison.description: Median rateable value changes across matched groups, England and Wales. The billing rules below apply to England.
valuation-comparison.note: The earlier median change for pubs was a 22.4% fall from 2017 to 2023. The published 2017 to 2026 comparison shows a 4.1% rise. These are valuation comparisons.

bill-example.title: How the same pub can have a higher valuation and a lower bill
bill-example.description: Illustration published by the Government for an independent pub. The first bar is the previous bill. The remaining bars are steps in the new bill.
bill-example.note: The example uses the 2025–26 and 2026–27 rules and whole-pound rounding. Bars are amounts at each step and should not be added.

valuation-jump.title: An upward revaluation can come as a shock after the COVID-era list
valuation-jump.text: The Government’s review reports a median pub valuation rise of 32.8% in England and Wales between the 2023 and 2026 lists. It identifies the end of COVID-era adjustments as a factor. The long comparison with 2017 shows a 4.1% rise across that wider period.
valuation-jump.evidenceGap: The published valuation distribution does not show how many operators paid a higher net bill after relief, or how those changes were distributed by type of pub.
valuation-jump.measure: Publish the distribution of net bill changes for pubs by area and valuation band, and the time taken to resolve checks and challenges.

improvement.title: Review the way pubs are valued
improvement.status: The call for evidence asks whether the present method properly reflects how pubs and hotels are valued and invites evidence on alternatives. Its publication does not change the current rating list.

consequences.text: An operator planning cash flow from the old valuation can face a different amount once the council recalculates the bill. If the property information or valuation is in dispute, there is a separate check and challenge process.

bill-complexity.title: A valuation figure leaves out the caps and discounts that determine the bill
bill-complexity.text: In the official example the pub’s rateable value rises from £30,000 to £39,000. The gross bill at the new 38.2p multiplier is £14,898. The eligible transitional cap takes this to £10,329, then the pub relief takes the bill down to £8,780.
bill-complexity.measure: Check the share of eligible properties receiving the discount, corrected bills and how quickly ratepayers receive them.

improvement.title: Increase the pub relief from April 2027
improvement.status: The October Budget announced a 35% discount from April 2027 for eligible pubs and other covered properties, up from 15%. The detailed package includes further changes to support and multipliers.

consequences.text: One missing relief can materially change what the operator is asked to pay. The City of London directs a pub that appears eligible but has not received the relief to its business rates team.

valuation-method.question: Does the current valuation method reflect the way pubs trade?
valuation-method.answer: The commissioned review published the valuation history and asked for evidence about how the fair maintainable trade approach works in practice. The call for evidence sets out the questions for the review. It does not settle them.
valuation-method.watch: Follow the published conclusions, any decision to change the method, and what that would do to valuations and bills after relief.

takeaways.label: The valuation
takeaways.text: The review reports median pub rateable values rose by 32.8% between the 2023 and 2026 revaluations in England and Wales, following a fall between the preceding revaluations.

takeaways.label: The bill
takeaways.text: England’s applicable multiplier and reliefs can offset a valuation rise. In the Government’s worked example, the valuation rose 30% while the bill fell from £8,982 to £8,780.

takeaways.label: The next change
takeaways.text: The October 2026 Budget announced a move from 15% to 35% pub relief from April 2027 in England. Keep this separate from the current year’s bill.

how-it-works.heading: Why the 2026 revaluation was different
how-it-works.text: The April 2023 list used an April 2021 valuation date, when COVID restrictions severely affected the evidence available from pubs. The Valuation Office adjusted pre-COVID trading evidence for those conditions. The April 2026 list uses an April 2024 valuation date, after restrictions had ended.

outcomes.heading: What the worked example shows
outcomes.text: In the worked example the finished bill falls by £202, about 2.2%, despite the 30% rise in valuation. What another pub pays depends on its rateable value, multiplier, previous relief and eligibility. The example demonstrates the calculation and gives no estimate of a typical bill change.

outcomes.heading: What would show a change for pubs
outcomes.text: Rates are one part of a pub’s costs. To assess the effect of the policy on trading and survival, compare net bills with outcomes for similar businesses and account for other changes in costs and demand. Valuation changes and pub closures alone cannot establish that effect.

cost-and-funding.heading: Who bears the cost of relief
cost-and-funding.text: Ratepayers pay the bill to the council. The 2026–27 guidance sets out how central government reimburses councils for qualifying relief through grants. The October 2026 Budget scores the higher relief for pubs, social clubs and eligible live music venues at £160 million in 2027–28 and £115 million in 2028–29. These are forecast Exchequer effects for the combined measure.

whats-changing.heading: What to check in April 2027
whats-changing.text: Check for the outcome of the valuation review and the guidance councils use to apply the 2027–28 package. After bills are issued, look for actual net changes across a spread of pubs and councils.
